newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Politics and power a big part of Gazprom shake-up.
newsitem.headline: Politics and power a big part of Gazprom shake-up.

text.p: Russia's giant natural gas monopoly Gazprom has been thrown into the centre of Moscow's political arena, as young reformers and old company stalwarts alike flex their muscles and promise change for the better.

The government wants to free up Russia's gas market and restructure the Soviet-era behemoth into a slick, money-spinning operation. Paradoxically, it sees the best way of doing this as reasserting state control over the company.
The company's management agrees on the basic course of change set out for Gazprom, but will not welcome attempts by fresh-faced reformers in the cabinet to take control.

Gazprom chairman Rem Vyakhirev and the goverment's economic guru, Minister without Portfolio Yevgeny Yasin, presented a united front on Thursday, giving the clearest vision yet of the future for the world's biggest gas producer.
"Gazprom, the government and the Fuel and Energy Ministry will work together on a number of issues, including introducing competition," Yasin told a news briefing.
He added that all parties would work towards strengthening the company's position on the world energy stage and increasing share value.
But Yasin pulled no punches about the size of the task.
"It will be difficult to introduce, and this will be done gradually," Yasin said, adding Gazprom controlled 95 percent of the Russian gas market and was still a strong monopoly.

Reducing wholesale gas prices, increasing transparency, hiving off huge and unwieldy non-core businesses and separating output, marketing, transport and finance are all part of the restructuring plan agreed on by the government and the company.

In an upbeat assessment of the company's future, Vyakhirev said that some of these changes had already been set out in concrete plans, and that the fruits of reform would be seen as early as next year.
"By 1998 this company should start to take on a more normal form, in line with international standards," he said.
The single, most politically sensitive issue during a highly public debate on the future of Gazprom in recent months has been the question of whether Gazprom will be broken up.
Both the government and the management have been careful to make clear that this was not an option.
Vyakhirev also stressed the need on Thursday to limit the amount of foreign control in the company, currently capped at nine percent.
He slammed what he called non-resident "swindlers" who he said had bought Gazprom shares on the domestic stock market, profiting by translating them into more valuable assets abroad.

Gazprom is trying to keep a strict separation between its domestic shares and the limited amount of equity available to investors outside Russia, which trades at premium of three times the local stock.

Also hitting the headlines this month has been the tussle for control of the government's 40 percent stake in the company between Vyakhirev and new reformist wonder-boy First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov.

Vyakhirev was handed personal control of seven eighths of the stake in 1993, but the shares' performance and the performance of the company as a whole have been criticised by Nemtsov, charged with revamping Russia's natural monopolies.

Even after protracted behind-the-scenes negotiations, Nemtsov and Vyakhirev have failed to reach a final compromise. Vyakhirev said on Thursday that the company has not yet put forward its proposed solution.
But there is little doubt that Nemtsov's star is in the ascendency at Gazprom, possibly at Vyakhirev's expense.
Nemtsov heads a committee set up by presidential decree, charged with reforming Gazprom. He will enjoy the backing of a formidable team of pre-reform and anti-monopoly representatives.
Where Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, former Gazprom head, stands in the great Gazprom debate remains unclear. So far he has been conspicuous only by his absence.
The stakes in Gazprom are high. Russia accounts for a third of the world's gas reserves and 27 percent of output. It is a key supplier to the Western European natural gas market.
Yet the company's debts to the state are huge, pegged by Nemtsov last month at 14.8 trillion roubles ($2.6 billion).
In response Gazprom blames the problem on even bigger debts owed to it for gas already supplied. These were estimated at 64 trillion roubles ($11.1 billion) as of early February.
